DOCUMENT:
Market Analysis: Launching a Digital Subscription for the Calderbrook Courier
Commercial Strategy, Calderbrook Media, April 2026

1. Purpose
The Calderbrook Courier's website is free to read and funded by display advertising, which has declined by about 12% a year for three years. This paper assesses the market for a metered digital subscription, in which readers can view five articles a month free before being asked to subscribe, and recommends a price and launch plan.

2. Our audience
The website had an average of 420,000 monthly unique users (MUU) in 2025, of whom around 60% live in the Courier's circulation area. The printed Courier has 11,200 subscribers paying £18.50 a month for six-day home delivery, plus around 6,000 daily news-stand sales. Print subscribers are older on average than web readers, and most also use the website.

In our March 2026 survey of print subscribers (1,850 responses), 30% said they would cancel their print subscription and take a digital-only subscription instead if one were offered at under £6 a month.

3. Evidence from comparable titles
We obtained data, under confidentiality agreements, from four regional titles that launched metered subscriptions between 2022 and 2024.

Table 1. Comparable regional titles, second year after launch
Title | Monthly unique users | Digital subscribers | Subscribers as % of MUU | Monthly price
Title A | 360,000 | 6,800 | 1.9% | £5.99
Title B | 280,000 | 3,100 | 1.1% | £4.99
Title C | 390,000 | 9,400 | 2.4% | £7.99
Title D | 300,000 | 4,200 | 1.4% | £3.99

All four titles reported that subscriber numbers stabilised by the end of the second year, and that churn settled at between 3% and 5% a month after promotional periods ended.

4. Price
Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices, which suggests that our audience will respond best to a low price point. We therefore propose a price of £4.99 a month, with an introductory offer of £1 for the first three months.

5. Projection
The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU. Applied to our 420,000 MUU, that gives about 8,400 subscribers by the end of year two. At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue.

Table 2. Year-two projection
Item | Annual amount
Subscription revenue | £503,000
Subscription platform and payment fees | £85,000
Marketing | £60,000
Net contribution | £358,000

We expect a modest reduction in display advertising revenue as page views from non-subscribers fall when they reach the meter; the comparable titles reported falls of 5% to 8% in page views. Our display revenue was £1.1 million in 2025, so a fall of this size would cost between £55,000 and £88,000 a year, which is well covered by the projected net contribution.

6. Launch plan
- Platform selection and integration: May to July 2026.
- Soft launch with a ten-article meter: September 2026.
- Full launch with a five-article meter: November 2026.
- Review of price and meter after six months.

7. Conclusion
The evidence from comparable titles shows a viable market for a Courier digital subscription. At £4.99 a month, a price that the comparable titles' experience suggests will maximise take-up, we project around 8,400 subscribers and a net contribution of £358,000 a year, more than offsetting the expected effect on display advertising. We recommend approval to proceed with the launch plan.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU." -- (1.9 + 1.1 + 2.4 + 1.4) / 4 = 1.7%, not 2.0%. At 1.7% the projection is about 7,140 subscribers, not 8,400, and revenue about £428,000.
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices" -- Table 1 shows the opposite pattern: the highest-priced title (C, £7.99) has the highest conversion (2.4%) and the lowest-priced (D, £3.99) has 1.4%. The pricing rationale rests on misreading the table.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue." -- The projection treats all subscription revenue as incremental, but the document's own survey says 30% of the 11,200 print subscribers (about 3,360) would cancel £18.50 print subscriptions for a digital one under £6. Switching would cost about £13.51 a month each (roughly £545,000 a year), which is never addressed although it could wipe out the net contribution.

REVIEW:
# Review: Calderbrook Courier Digital Subscription Market Analysis

Using comparable titles is a sound approach, and the paper is clear and well structured. However, two of its three central claims don't hold up against its own data, and the largest financial risk, cannibalisation of print, is missing from the projection. As written, the recommendation is not supported.

## 1. The "highest conversion at the lowest price" claim is the reverse of what Table 1 shows

Sorted by price:

| Title | Price | Conversion |
|---|---|---|
| D | £3.99 | 1.4% |
| B | £4.99 | **1.1%** |
| A | £5.99 | 1.9% |
| C | £7.99 | **2.4%** |

The most expensive title converts best. The only title already at £4.99 converts worst. If the table suggests anything, it is that higher prices did not hurt take-up.

Four data points can't establish a price effect in either direction. Content strength, local competition and meter design are all confounders. But the paper's stated rationale for £4.99 is contradicted by its own evidence, so Section 4 and the conclusion both need rewriting. The data also gives no reason to rule out £5.99–£7.99, which would raise revenue per subscriber by 20–60%.

## 2. The average conversion rate is 1.7%, not 2.0%

- Simple mean: (1.9 + 1.1 + 2.4 + 1.4) / 4 = **1.7%**
- Pooled (23,500 subscribers ÷ 1.33m MUU): **1.77%**

Corrected projection:

| | Paper | At 1.7% | At Title B's 1.1% (same price) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Subscribers | 8,400 | 7,140 | 4,620 |
| Subscription revenue | £503k | £428k | £277k |
| Net contribution (fees scaled pro rata, marketing £60k) | £358k | ~£296k | ~£170k |

The Title B case deserves explicit treatment. It is the only comparable at the proposed price.

## 3. Print cannibalisation is the biggest omission

Section 2 reports that 30% of surveyed print subscribers would switch to digital-only at under £6. Yet this never appears in the projection:

- 30% × 11,200 = 3,360 switchers
- Revenue lost per switcher: £18.50 − £4.99 = £13.51/month
- 3,360 × £13.51 × 12 = **~£545,000 a year**

That exceeds the entire projected net contribution. Stated intent overstates actual behaviour, so the real figure would be lower. Still, even a third of it (~£180k) would remove most of the corrected margin.

Two further points:
- The comparison should use print **contribution**, not revenue. Switchers save printing and delivery costs, so finance needs to supply the per-subscriber print margin.
- Switchers would sit inside the digital subscriber count, so some of the 7,000–8,400 are not new revenue at all.

This is also a pricing argument. A low digital price widens the gap with print and encourages switching. That is another reason to reconsider £4.99.

## 4. Smaller issues

- **Display loss sits outside Table 2.** The author's summary says it was "explicitly costed", but it should appear as a line in the net figure. Display has been falling 12% a year, so the 2028 base will be nearer £750k than £1.1m. That actually makes this line smaller. Also, a 5–8% fall in page views doesn't necessarily mean a proportional revenue fall, because subscribers are often the most valuable ad audience.
- **Churn and marketing.** At 3–5% monthly churn, holding 7,000–8,400 subscribers means replacing roughly 210–420 a month. The paper should show that £60k a year is enough to achieve this.
- **Introductory offer.** £1 for three months lowers year-one revenue. The paper should include a year-one view as well as the year-two steady state.
- **Comparability.** Only 60% of Courier users are local. Do the comparables have similar local shares? Non-local users rarely subscribe, so if the comparables are more local, Courier conversion could come in lower.
- **Phased launch.** A ten-article meter for two months, followed by the review six months after full launch, leaves little room to "learn before committing". Set explicit go/adjust criteria for the soft-launch period, such as a conversion threshold and print switching rates.

## 5. Recommended revisions

1. Correct the average to 1.7% and present a range of scenarios (1.1%, 1.7%, 2.4%).
2. Remove the claim that a low price maximises take-up. Reconsider the price, perhaps testing £5.99 or more.
3. Add a print cannibalisation line using print contribution margin, and test sensitivity to switching rates of 10%, 20% and 30%.
4. Put display loss and churn-driven acquisition costs into the main projection table.
5. Add measurable decision criteria to the soft launch.

The case for a digital subscription may well survive these changes. But the conclusion that it "comfortably covers" its costs depends on an arithmetic error, a misreading of the price data, and leaving out the print impact. The paper needs revision before it goes for approval.
